extracted.intended_audience: aspiring young authors and careful readers of philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and philosophical advice for youthful literati: how to organize a writing life (whether and when to make authorship a profession) and how to approach and judge philosophical writings. Contains prescriptions about employment, motives, self-examination, reading practice, and audience-suitability for difficult philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never pursue literature as a trade
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make authorship your sole profession; instead secure some regular employment from which three hours of leisure, free from alien anxieties, will enable more genial and substantial literary product than weeks of compulsion. Money and immediate reputation are arbitrary ends that can convert stimulants into narcotics; the necessity of acquiring them will 'stun and stupify the mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide talents and genius: acquire competence in a profession
rubrics_metrics.description: “devote his talents to the acquirement of competence in some known trade or profession, and his genius to objects of his tranquil and unbiassed choice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a practical profession to secure competence and independence; reserve creative genius for free, unpressured pursuits. This division ennobles both activities and prevents vanity/indolence from masquerading as humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three hours of leisure suffice for genial production
rubrics_metrics.description: “Three hours of leisure, unannoyed by any alien anxiety, and looked forward to with delight as a change and recreation, will suffice to realize in literature a larger product of what is truly genial, than weeks of compulsion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, regular, undisturbed periods devoted to writing while engaging in other employment are preferable to making writing a pressured full-time occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer an established profession (e.g., the Church) to secure literary freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church presents to every man of learning and genius a profession, in which he may cherish a rational hope of being able to unite the widest schemes of literary utility with the strictest performance of professional duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An established profession—particularly the clergy—is commended because it situates the literary person within society (neighbor, family-man), provides patronage, moral decorum, and occasions for intellectual interests across many departments; it avoids some temptations and supplies social utility and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be not merely a man of letters
rubrics_metrics.description: “be not merely a man of letters! Let literature be an honourable augmentation to your arms; but not constitute the coat, or fill the escutcheon!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain other social and professional identities (husband, father, professional) so that you are not judged solely as an author; this broadness of role preserves sympathy with the world, improves tact, and protects domestic happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examine scruples before embracing authorship; delay if doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let him catalogue his scruples, and reduce them to a distinct intelligible form; let him be certain, that he has read with a docile mind and favourable dispositions the best and most fundamental works on the subject... Time spent in such delay is time won: for manhood in the meantime is advancing...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before renouncing other employment for literature, perform strict self-scrutiny to ensure doubts are not laziness, restlessness, or vain impatience; read foundational works and consult older contemporaries who faced similar doubts. A delaying period often matures judgment and temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing every thought; guard against becoming a mere servant of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Herder: “Am sorgfaeltigsten, meiden sie die Autorschaft. Zu frueh oder unmaessig gebraucht, macht sie den Kopf wueste and das Herz leer... und wer jeden Gedanken, der ihm aufstosst, durch Feder and Presse versendet, hat sie in kurzer Zeit alle versandt, und wird bald ein blosser Diener der Druckerey, ein Buchstabensetzer werden.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exercise authorship immoderately or prematurely; excessive publication empties head and heart and reduces the writer to a mere mechanic of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presume yourself ignorant of a writer's understanding until you understand his ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: “until you understand a writer’s ignorance, presume yourself ignorant of his understanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading philosophical works, first seek to grasp the limits and errors (the 'ignorance') that shape an author's views; only then can you judge what understanding the author actually possesses. This humility avoids mistaking jargon or opacity for profundity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read philosophical chapters connectedly; avoid isolated excerpts
rubrics_metrics.description: “either pass over the following chapter altogether, or read the whole connectedly. The fairest part of the most beautiful body will appear deformed and monstrous, if dissevered from its place in the organic whole.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extract or sample delicate philosophical passages out of context; such disconnection can present a skeleton or deform the author's thought—read the larger organic whole to understand subtle distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary criterion for whether a reader will profit from a philosophical chapter
rubrics_metrics.description: “if a man receives as fundamental facts... the general notions of matter, spirit, soul, body, action, passiveness, time, space, cause and effect, consciousness, perception, memory and habit; if he feels his mind completely at rest concerning all these... to such a mind I would... convey the hint, that for him the chapter was not written.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reader treats the listed general notions as fixed, indemonstrable fundamentals and is satisfied reducing other notions to them, that reader will likely find the philosophical chapter unhelpful. The author warns readers to self-assess before reading difficult, transcendental material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy in the highest sense is intelligible only to those with cultivated transcendental consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a philosophic... consciousness... behind the spontaneous consciousness... The latter is exclusively the domain of pure philosophy, which is therefore properly entitled transcendental... it must in truth be a land of darkness for men to whom the noblest treasures of their own being are reported only through... lifeless and sightless motions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True philosophy requires an inner, disciplined intuition beyond ordinary reflection; those lacking this cultivated 'immediate' consciousness will find transcendental philosophy obscure or unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of mistaking mere analysis of terms for real philosophical advance
rubrics_metrics.description: “This mere analysis of terms is preparative only, though as a preparative discipline indispensable... For philosophy in its highest sense... this mere analysis of terms... does not really add to it. It does not increase, though it gives us a greater mastery over, the wealth which we before possessed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic exercises and terminological reduction are useful preparations but not substitutes for substantive philosophical insight; do not overvalue forensic or professional mastery of terms as equivalent to ultimate philosophical knowledge.
